fatal_errors: The proposed AlCoCrFeNi2.1 L12-forming interlayer is not the studied material or intervention; the target is an Al-Cr-Fe-Ni FCC/BCC multilayer with a 16 nm modulation period and semicoherent interfaces.

The hypothesis substitutes elevated-temperature testing and a temperature-driven mechanism transition for the target's room-temperature nanoindentation creep and interface-coherency-driven transition.
It identifies coherent interfaces as the key mediator, whereas the reported transition and strongest creep resistance occur at semicoherent interfaces containing misfit dislocations.

The proposed mechanism is inconsistent with the target: semicoherent-interface dislocation pileup and possible interfacial amorphization promote diffusion/interface slip, while coherent and grain-boundary-dominated samples show dislocation-mediated creep.
The sole cited evidence concerns molten-salt corrosion of bulk AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and provides no support for creep, an L12 interlayer, interface coherency, or the proposed mechanism transition.
explanation: The response recognizes the broad topic of interface-controlled creep in HEA multilayers and proposes a testable comparative experiment, but it does not reconstruct the reported system or result. The relevant material is the approximately 1 μm Al-Cr-Fe-Ni FCC/BCC multilayer with a 16 nm layer period (M16), whose semicoherent interfaces produce the minimum stress exponent and strongest reported room-temperature creep resistance. The generated hypothesis instead invents a coherent L12-like AlCoCrFeNi2.1 interlayer and an elevated-temperature transition. Its evidence is unrelated corrosion work, so the central material choice and mechanistic claims are unsupported despite a reasonably discriminating experimental design.
